Title: Pahang coastline needs early action as erosion risks grow
Article:
KUANTAN: Pahang's direct exposure to South China Sea makes its coastline increasingly vulnerable to stronger waves and extreme weather, highlighting the need for early action to tackle coastal erosion.
Universiti Malaysia Terengganu  Associate Professor  Dr Effi Helmy Ariffin said unlike parts of Terengganu where offshore islands provided some protection from the open sea, Pahang's coastline was more directly exposed to severe weather.
"There can be typhoons, cyclones and other  extreme weather events. The effects of coastal erosion are gradual but becoming increasingly visible, particularly along the southern part of Pahang.
"Pekan, including Nenasi and Rompin, are among the areas showing signs of coastal erosion."
The coastal erosion expert said early intervention was vital because timely action could prevent more serious and costly damage in the future.
He  proposed a hybrid approach combining breakwaters and artificial reefs.
He described it as the best way forward given the difficulty of predicting conditions in the South China Sea.
"The hybrid concept involves positioning the reefs between the breakwaters.
"For long-term planning, we need a more sustainable approach, while short-term measures can include armour rock or other forms of coastal protection."
Effi Helmy also highlighted the role of sediment movement in maintaining beaches, particularly when sand was removed from river estuaries for flood mitigation and navigation.
"Sand obtained through dredging could be considered for replenishing beaches affected by erosion, subject to proper   assessment of the sediment's suitability.
"Soft solutions such as beach nourishment can be adopted alongside other coastal protection measures."
Environmentalist Dr Muhamad Rusdi Ahmad Rusmili said studies of coastal and river-mouth hydrodynamics (the movement of water) were crucial to understanding and managing coastal erosion, as changes in water flow could affect sediment movement and accelerate shoreline loss.
The Malaysian Nature Society (MNS) Pahang branch chairman said seemingly minor factors could have significant consequences for coastal areas, making it important to examine water movement, river systems and the interaction between waves, sediment and the coastline.
He said Pahang's east coast was particularly vulnerable during the northeast monsoon, when strong winds and waves could transport sand offshore and intensify coastal erosion.
"Beserah is among the areas at risk of  coastal erosion.
"Concrete barriers and wave breakers could offer protection in certain circumstances, but such measures should  be implemented only after  studies are conducted to assess their potential effects on surrounding areas.
"Development is necessary, but it has to be done properly. We do not want a situation where protecting one area causes problems somewhere else."
Rusdi said environmental impact assessments and other technical studies should consider a broad range of factors before coastal development projects are allowed to proceed.
These should include hydrodynamics, sediment movement, river discharge, wave patterns and the potential impact of coastal structures on neighbouring stretches of coastline.
He said an  understanding of these factors would help ensure that efforts to protect vulnerable areas did not inadvertently worsen erosion elsewhere.
Rusdi said MNS carried out mangrove restoration and coastal tree-planting programmes where conditions were suitable, particularly where mangroves could help stabilise the shoreline and reduce erosion.
"Not every coastal area is suitable for mangrove planting, as the success of restoration depends on factors such as soil conditions, water movement and the characteristics of river mouths."

Title: Pahang seeks RM850m to tackle erosion along 61km coastline
Article:
KUANTAN: The Pahang government has implemented short- and long-term measures to address coastal erosion  along  61km of coastline in the Pekan, Rompin and Kuantan districts.
State Public Works, Transport and Health Committee chairman Datuk  Razali Kassim said the  Irrigation and Drainage Department  conducted studies and kept records to identify the   causes of coastal erosion and determine  appropriate measures.
He said coastal erosion was a year-round issue requiring continuous monitoring and action, particularly  where it could affect  homes, public infrastructure and access routes.
"Various engineering approaches are being considered, depending on the conditions
and characteristics of each location.
"Some problems can be resolved quickly, while major works will take longer.
"At some locations, temporary repairs and mitigation measures have  been carried out to prevent further damage while longer-term solutions are being  considered."
He said the Pahang Integrated Shoreline Management Plan, led by the Irrigation and Drainage Department and completed last year, identified several factors contributing to coastal erosion.
These included  development activities, sand mining, the natural loss of sandbars and mud,  mangrove loss and large waves coinciding with high tides.
Razali said some stretches of the coastal road between Pekan and Rompin, including Padang Api-Api in Nenasi, had been affected by erosion.
"Apart from short-term measures to address the worsening  erosion along the stretch, we are also considering  realigning the road as part of long-term infrastructure improvements."
He said the Pahang government, through the Irrigation and Drainage Department, had requested  RM850 million under the 13th Malaysia Plan for coastal erosion control, estuary conservation and related mitigation works.

Title: Waves sweep away home, memories in Rompin village [WATCH]
Article:
ROMPIN:   The Malay proverb, "
kalau takut dilambung ombak, jangan berumah di tepi pantai
" (if you are afraid of being hit by waves, do not live by the beach), has taken on a painful meaning for Nur Zakiah Hamdan, whose family lost their home in Kampung Jawa here to coastal erosion last year.
The three-room house was sponsored by a financial institution for her family in 2009. They did not expect giant waves during the monsoon season on Jan 12 last year to bring down one of its walls, forcing them to leave the village.
The 30-year-old said the incident had a profound impact on her family, especially her father, Hamdan Mohid, 61, who would shed tears each time he visited the damaged house, now riddled with cracks and rusting window frames.
"Our home held so many memories. It had a verandah facing the sea where my whole family would spend our evenings watching the waves and enjoying the sea breeze... it was where my youngest brother was born, and where I lost my mother and a brother to illness.
"Everything was taken away in a single night, when the waves repeatedly crashed against the walls, sweeping away our furniture and electrical appliances.
"Just hours earlier, we were told to move to a nearby relief centre with several neighbours," she said when met recently.
The housewife said the house might have been spared if preventive measures had been taken earlier to slow the erosion.
"When I moved here, the shoreline was about 500m from my house. During the incident last year, the sea was barely 20m away. The huge casuarina trees and the tarred road in front of my house have disappeared.
"Over the years, the  trees collapsed one after another due to the powerful waves before the road was eventually swept away.
"Sadly, no erosion barrier was built until last year, when geotubes were placed along the coastline... it was already too late," she said.
Nur Zakiah, who now lives in a rented house in the nearby Kampung Janglau, said she still vividly remembered the night her family's home was damaged.
She was at the relief centre  on the night of Jan 12 last year when her husband told her  the walls of their house had collapsed.
"I went back to inspect the house. The electricity had been shut off and most of our belongings had been washed away by the strong waves. Luckily, we managed to rescue some documents before moving to the relief centre," she said, adding that losses were estimated at more than RM20,000.
Azman Jumahir, who lives in the same village, said villagers used to be wary of huge waves only during the monsoon season, but now they had to be on alert  throughout the year, especially during high tide.
The 30-year-old, who grew up in the village, said such incidents had become more frequent over the past few years, with huge waves sweeping debris and plastic bottles into the settlement.
"During high tide, the waves enter my house, which is about 100m from the shoreline. Since 2023, we have been told to evacuate during the monsoon season... not because of floods, but because of huge waves," he said.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: MLS fines Messi for striking an opponent
Article:
MIAMI: Major League Soccer fined Inter Miami's Argentine superstar Lionel Messi an undisclosed amount on Friday for slapping Philadelphia's Quinn Sullivan on the back of the neck in the clubs' 2-2 draw on Wednesday.
The league's disciplinary committee said it had levied the fine "for violating the league's policy regarding hands to the face/head/neck of an opponent."
Miami's Ian Fray was fined an undisclosed amount for the same infraction.
It was late in stoppage time of a testy contest when Messi approached the center circle to confront Sullivan while the ball was in play in another area of the field.
After a brief exchange, Messi took a swipe at Sullivan, who then squared up to the Argentine star in a fight-style stare-down.
Referee Filip Dujic, who had his back turned during the incident, arrived to separate the players but did not show either of them a card.
Dujic did send off Cavan Sullivan, younger brother and teammate of Quinn, and Miami's Italian midfielder Yannick Bright after their stoppage time scuffle in Miami's penalty area.

Title: RM700,000 seaside dream swept away by coastal erosion [WATCH]
Article:
PEKAN:    A businessman's dream of turning a stretch of the coast in Tanjung Batu here into a unique seaside retreat was all but swept away by the relentless advance of the sea.
Tourism entrepreneur Edde Firdaus Abdul Aziz had invested some RM700,000 to acquire 1ha of coastal land, transforming it into Kekunang Tering Chalet, a nature getaway featuring seven chalets, including a tree house and tube cabins fashioned from concrete culverts.
But the dream lasted only about six years before relentless coastal erosion claimed the structures one by one.
The chalet units were swept into the sea in late 2022.
Edde Firdaus, 46, said the sea had since devoured much of the land, leaving just 0.4ha, with the remaining ground continuing to disappear.
"It's heartbreaking to see the chalet units disappear one by one. I only managed to operate the business for about six years before it was all swept away.
"Now, only the concrete culverts remain visible, partially buried in sand. The four concrete rooms were built furthest from the shoreline, so you can imagine the extent of the destruction," he said.
Edde Firdaus said after securing the land, he spent close to half a million ringgit on premium construction materials, including high-quality glass and furniture.
"I managed to salvage some furniture, electrical appliances and mattresses, but the structures were washed away. I never imagined that the land could disappear like this.
"When I bought the land, the ground was covered in grass, acacia trees and mangroves, while the shoreline was quite a distance away.
"Even when erosion began, I tried various methods, including placing giant sandbags to hold back the sea, but when the tree house collapsed, I knew trouble was closing in," he said.
Edde Firdaus claimed the beach erosion-control project in nearby Kampung Tanjung Batu, completed in March, appeared to have accelerated erosion along his property.
"Perhaps changes in the wave pattern and water flow contributed to the severe erosion. In the past, coastal erosion usually happened during the monsoon season, but now it happens throughout the year.
"I am just  waiting for the monsoon season this year. The extreme weather could wipe out what remains of my land," he said.
Former staff member Abdul Manan Md Amin, 61, who accompanied the
New Straits Times
to the site, said the chalets were unoccupied when they were washed away.
"It had been forecast that there would be high tide that night, so I was monitoring the site. The waves kept pounding the chalets and, the following morning, we saw that most of the structures had been washed away," he said.

Title: Trump announces temporary tariff relief on ground beef imports
Article:
WASHINGTON: President Donald Trump announced on Friday that the United States would temporarily allow a greater volume of foreign beef imports, in his latest bid to lower costs for American consumers as midterm elections approach.
The US cattle herd has shrunk to its lowest level since the 1950s – in part due to drought and international competition – with the diminishing numbers pushing beef product prices higher.
"As we work to rebuild this herd and help our ranchers, for the next 90 days, the United States will allow up to 300,000 metric tons of product for ground beef to be imported with no out-of-quota tariff," Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform.
The US president did not say which countries would be exporting the beef, but added there was a commitment to sell it at 25 per cent below market prices.
Steeper beef prices have become a symbol of high living costs in the world's biggest economy, pressing the Trump administration to take steps to bring costs down.
Affordability will be a key issue in November's midterm elections, where Democrats are seeking to wrest control of both houses of Congress from Trump's Republicans.
'DISAPPOINTED'
US cattle and rancher groups have been resistant to importing more beef. Responding to the move, Senator Deb Fischer of Nebraska, a major beef-producing state, said she was "extremely disappointed".
"We all want lower grocery prices, but as I've said for months, we cannot do it at the expense of American producers. Flooding the market with foreign beef hurts our livestock industry," said Fischer, a Republican.
[[nid:1516327]]
Responding to the criticism later in the day, Trump offered no details on how the plan would work but insisted that he would get beef prices down because "that's what the voters want, and that's what I want".
Last fall, Trump demanded that ranchers slash their prices, and he later moved to expand imports of beef trimmings from Argentina to cool ground beef prices.
He has also launched an investigation into the meatpacking industry over the high prices of red meat.
His latest effort comes as American households struggle with stubborn inflation, fuelled by an energy crisis linked to the war on Iran.
Trump launched the war alongside ally Israel in late February, with Teheran's retaliatory action virtually blocking the Strait of Hormuz, a vital energy and fertiliser supply route.
This has pushed up fuel, transport and food costs, squeezing consumers.
Despite higher beef prices, US consumer demand for meat remains robust.
The US Department of Agriculture estimates that total beef consumption this year will hit 29.4 billion pounds, an uptick from 2025.
The American Farm Bureau Federation warned in May, however, that Americans are consuming more beef than US farmers and ranchers can supply.
It added that ranchers need to rebuild the US cattle herd – or demand would have to cool – in order for beef prices to fall.
Yet "cattle producers still face substantial uncertainty that clouds herd rebuilding decisions," Bernt Nelson, an economist at the federation, wrote.
These include threats to animal health, including the New World screwworm, a flesh-eating parasite.

Title: Pahang coastline under siege as erosion threatens homes, roads and livelihoods [WATCH]
Article:
KUANTAN:    Along Pahang's 210km coastline spanning three districts — Kuantan, Pekan and Rompin — the South China Sea is steadily reshaping the boundary between land and water, alarming coastal communities.
Metres of shoreline have been lost over the years, with beaches gradually disappearing, homes and livelihoods  under threat and growing fears that roads and other infrastructure could eventually be swallowed up by the sea.
Strong waves have severely damaged and eroded the shorelines of at least 10 locations in Pahang, including popular beaches Pantai Cherating and Teluk Chempedak, as well as beaches in Pekan and Rompin.
Other affected areas include Pantai Balok, Pantai Kempadang, Pantai Sepat and Pantai Cherok Paloh in Kuantan;  Tanjung Batu in Pekan; and Kuala Rompin, Tanjung Gemok and Kampung Mukut on Pulau Tioman in Rompin.
Sultan of Pahang Al-Sultan Abdullah Ri'ayatuddin Al-Mustafa Billah Shah raised concerns about the condition of the state's coastline last year after observing the extent of erosion during a helicopter tour.
[[nid:1516332]]
He singled out Padang Api-Api along the Jalan Pekan-Nenasi stretch in Pekan, where erosion had brought the main road closer to the coastline, warning that  the road could be swallowed up by waves within five years  if no action was taken.
In response, the Pahang government has submitted a request for RM4 million to build beach revetments and carry out beach nourishment and dredging works along the affected stretch.
Coastal erosion had also claimed the four-star Summerset Resort in Rompin, once a favourite holiday destination and haven for nature lovers.
The resort, which opened in 2000, closed about 12 years later after erosion along the coastline became increasingly severe.
Several years ago, the Pahang government proposed the construction of a rock revetment to cushion the impact of coastal erosion, but this required  about RM10 million to rehabilitate a 1km stretch.
Pahang has submitted an application for RM850 million under the 13th Malaysia Plan this year to carry out coastal erosion control, estuary conservation and related mitigation works.

Title: Rocky case, Maju Junction deaths and Singaporean kidnapping among key court cases this week
Article:
KLANG: A tussle between a volunteer dog-catcher and a housewife over a dog named Rocky on July 29 ended with both being charged with animal cruelty at the Klang Sessions Court on Thursday.
Rocky was believed to be a stray and was being caught during an enforcement operation when the woman claimed ownership of the male dog.
The ensuing confrontation turned tense, with Rocky secured by a loop rope, died during the incident.
On Thursday, parcel delivery rider Muhammad Shah Idham Nor Haikal Shaharom,24, was charged with unreasonably choking Rocky using a loop rope while and S. Roghini Devi, 42, was charged with unreasonably pulling it, causing pain to the animal.
Both pleaded not guilty to the alleged offence committed at Taman Telok Gedung Indah.
The offence carries a fine of between RM20,000 and RM100,000, jail for up to three years, or both.
Meanwhile, at the magistrate's court, Roghini pleaded guilty to failing to obtain a dog license for Rocky, an offence under Section 3 of the Klang Royal City Council's Dog Licensing and Dog Breeding House By-Laws.
This case received wide publicity as activists spoke up against animal cruelty. They held a street protest in Klang and were warned by police not to hold a similar demonstration outside the courthouse on Thurs.
Below are some of the other court cases reported this week.
The deaths of a father and his two daughters in a road accident at the Maju Junction intersection along Jalan Sultan Ismail on Wednesday, saw an Immigration Department lorry driver Mohd Akbar Zainol, 43, charged with causing death by reckless or dangerous driving.
He was brought before the magistrate's court to face five charges framed under several provisions of the Road Transport Act, following a one-day remand.
Akbar pleaded not guilty to three counts under Section 41(1) for allegedly causing the deaths of Shaik Mohd Firdaus Shaik Yahya, 53, and his two daughters, Siti Norshazlin, 25, and Siti Darwisyah Auni, 12.
The three victims died after the lorry driven by Akbar allegedly crashed into a Proton Saga before losing control and hitting them. Shaik Mohd Firdaus's wife, Nor Hayati Rozali was injured in the 1am incident.
Akbar was also charged under Section 43(1) of the same Act with driving without due care and attention, resulting in injuries to Nor Hayati.
The fifth charge, under Section 79(2) of the Act, alleged that Akbar failed to obey a red traffic light at the intersection.
In Batu Pahat, Johor, a devastated father in his 60s broke down as he witnessed four men being charged at the magistrate's court over the alleged murder of his 39-year-old son, Low Kai Xian.
Low had been reported missing before his body was found wrapped in a net and floating in Sungai Tanjung Sembrong, Parit Raja.
Lorry driver Yogesvaran Subramaniam, 40; lorry attendants Lim Yong Ming, 26, and Achuthan Nagarajan, 32; and used-car dealer How Han Wei, 33 were jointly charged with murdering Low.
The four were accused of murdering Low between an eatery in Jalan Emas Putih, Taman Sri Skudai, Johor Baru, and Sungai Tanjung Sembrong, between 2.35pm on July 29 and 12.30pm on Aug 3. It was believed to be over debts.
No plea was recorded as murder cases are under the jurisdiction of the High Court. They were denied bail.
In Johor Baru yesterday, six people, including a woman, were charged with kidnapping a Singaporean man and demanding RM63,000 in ransom earlier this month.
M. Balamurugam, 46, K. Saravanan, 40, P. Sri Devi, 41, G. Puganeswaran, 38, S. Gobinath, 38, and X. Adwin Nicholas, 41, pleaded not guilty to the charge.
The six allegedly kidnapped Al-Shameer Abdul Nassar with the intention of demanding S$20,000 (RM63,000) in ransom on Aug 8.
In a separate Magistrate's court here, all six also pleaded not guilty to jointly abducting a Singaporean woman.
The court granted bail of RM60,000 each to Sri Devi, Adwin Nicholas and Puganeswaran, while Balamurugam, Saravanan and Gobinath were granted bail of RM69,000 each, with local sureties.

Title: Genting heist, child trafficking, woman burnt among major crimes this week
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: Police are still hunting three masked men who made off with jewellery worth about RM1.7 million in a daring two-minute heist at a goldsmith in SkyAvenue, Genting Highlands, on Monday.
The brazen daylight robbery raised eyebrows because of the speed and precision with which the robbery was carried out.
Police activated Ops Tutup, setting up roadblocks at entry and exit points at the hilltop resort and along the route towards Batang Kali.
However, the suspects managed to evade the dragnet after CCTV footage showed the vehicle believed to have been used in the robbery had already passed a checkpoint before the roadblocks were activated. No arrests have been reported so far.
Below are some of the major crimes reported in the country this week.
In Klang, a gang of four men armed with sledgehammers and what appeared to be a firearm, fled empty-handed after their attempted robbery at a goldsmith's shop in Jalan Tengku Kelana went wrong on Thursday.
The suspects, who came on motorcycles, struck at the shop at about 10.30am but their repeated attempts to smash the display glass with the sledgehammers failed.
Another suspect was seen apparently brandishing an object resembling a pistol outside, who was later joined by the three, before they fled the scene.
Police rescued 17 Jordanian children aged between three months and 14 years believed to have been forced to beg at busy tourist and commercial areas in the city.
The victims, eight boys and nine girls, were rescued in a raid under Op Pintas Kasih launched on Aug 19, targeting a suspected foreign trafficking syndicate operating mainly in Bukit Bintang and Chow Kit.
Raids were conducted by Bukit Aman CID's Anti-Trafficking in Persons and Anti-Smuggling of Migrants Division (D3), resulting in the arrest of 15 adults as well, comprising seven men and eight women aged between the ages of 21 and 49.
Police believe the suspects, believed to be Jordanian nationals, generated between RM500 and RM1,000 daily by using the children to solicit money from the public.
They also seized 32 Jordanian passports, 14 mobile phones, four strollers and cash in various currencies amounting to more than RM25,000.
The suspects are being investigated under Section 14 of the Anti-Trafficking in Persons and Anti-Smuggling of Migrants Act 2007, which carries a maximum penalty of life imprisonment, as well as the Child Act 2001 and Immigration Act 1959/63.
Police arrested a 59-year-old man on Tuesday, who was believed to have seriously injured a victim at a lottery outlet in Kepong last week.
The suspect, an e-hailing driver, had allegedly doused a 62-year-old woman behind the counter with petrol before igniting her.
Investigations later revealed the motive for the attack was over lottery numbers. Police said that the suspect and the woman knew each other but there were no further details available.
The suspect was remanded for a week while the case is being investigated under Section 326 of the Penal Code for voluntarily causing grievous hurt using a dangerous weapon or means.

Title: Explainer: What we know about the door handles that triggered China's record auto recall
Article:
DETROIT: Electronic door handles of the kind at the centre of China's largest-ever vehicle recall have proliferated across the globe over the past decade, especially on electric vehicles.
Tesla and eight other automakers said on Friday they will recall a total of about 4.3 million vehicles in China over concerns that their doors may be difficult to open in an emergency.
Popularised by Tesla, the door handles are designed to sit flush with the body of the door, for a minimalist look that also reduces aerodynamic drag. The handles electronically extend outward, typically as the owner approaches the car.
It is unclear whether Tesla plans to do a similar recall in the US or Europe. The company and auto safety regulators in the US and Europe did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
WHAT ARE THE CONCERNS WITH THESE HANDLES?
Vehicle doors with these handles employ buttons to open them rather than a traditional mechanical system.
If automakers do not have a clear manual release option in case a car loses power, it can be difficult for passengers or the driver to escape a vehicle in a life-threatening situation, said Michael Brooks, executive director of the Center for Auto Safety.
While some automakers have a relatively intuitive system in which an interior lever can be pulled twice to manually release the door, Tesla's manual release is either in the door pocket or under a panel, without clear signage, he said.
WHAT DO CAR OWNERS THINK?
Some EV drivers have found the evolving design of high-tech handles confusing.
"The basic touch point of door handles is now a percolating problem area as manufacturers attempt to redesign them," consultants JD Power said in 2023, stating that seven of the 10 most problematic models in this area were EVs.
[[nid:1516344]]
Several lawsuits have alleged that Tesla's door-handle designs led to driver or passenger injuries or deaths after they were trapped in a vehicle while it was on fire.
Some drivers have also complained to the US National Highway Traffic Safety Administration about being unable to get their child out of a vehicle after exiting.
WHAT VEHICLES ARE INVOLVED IN THE RECALL?
Tesla and several other automakers, including Xiaomi, launched software updates on Friday and said they would recall nearly 4.3 million vehicles over concerns that it may be difficult to open doors in an emergency.
Leapmotor, Xpeng and Geely also announced their largest recalls on record.
Reuters was unable to get an exact count of models using these electronic handles globally, but automakers have rolled out the design on dozens of new EV models globally in recent years.
WHAT ARE REGULATORS DOING?
China has increased oversight of the EV industry this year and in February said it would ban "hidden" door handles from 2027, the first country to take this step.
In the US, proposed legislation would order cars with this kind of handle to also carry a manual door release that is fail-safe.
The NHTSA said in July that the door release problem should be addressed by potentially creating a new formal safety standard that would apply to all automakers.
The decision came after the regulator reviewed a petition seeking a recall of Tesla Model 3 sedans over concerns that emergency door release controls may not be clear in an emergency. The NHTSA denied the petition in favour of addressing the issue through rulemaking.
Last year, European regulators flagged the potential risks involving door-handle designs as a key priority.
The United Nations Economic Commission for Europe has been drafting new standards to ensure that electronic handles can be opened from inside and out if the car's electricity is cut off.
A recall in one country does not necessarily mean an automaker would do the same in other markets, Brooks said.
"There remains a possibility here that Tesla will fight a recall in the United States," he said.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: US, Canada push to seal trade deal as deadline nears
Article:
WASHINGTON: US and Canadian negotiators raced against the clock on Friday to reach a trade deal before a midnight deadline when punishing new US tariffs are set to kick in.
In the latest salvo amid months of trade hostility, US President Donald Trump threatened to impose new 50 per cent duties on a range of Canadian products by Wednesday. But he issued a last-minute delay, citing major progress in trade talks.
Hours before the new deadline, Trump said the US "should be able to have a deal with Canada", citing his "good relationship" with Prime Minister Mark Carney.
Canadian negotiators have been camped out in Washington this week trying to finalise a deal that reportedly aims to address a range of flash points.
Both sides have said a pact is nearly done, but talks were continuing on Friday, with top Canadian negotiator Dominic LeBlanc meeting US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer.
Canada wants relief from Trump's tariffs on autos, steel and aluminium, which have battered Canada's economy, forced job losses and strained what was once an iron-clad trade relationship.
Details of the proposed agreement emerged this week after Carney briefed the leaders of Canada's provinces and territories.
US tariffs will likely be reduced in certain areas, but not removed entirely, with Saskatchewan's Conservative Premier Scott Moe telling reporters there's no going back to the pre-Trump "status quo".
Ryan Majerus, a trade lawyer at King & Spalding, told AFP that Washington's apparent willingness to reduce the sector-specific tariffs "dramatically increases the potential of a deal".
"I think both sides want an off-ramp here," Majerus said, while noting that Ottawa was "under tremendous pressure" to get tariffs removed and the public may be unhappy with the outcome.
Canada's opposition Conservative Party was already on the offensive on Friday, with its leader Pierre Poilievre saying "one-sided tariffs on Canadian industry would be a bad deal".
"Tell me how the Canadian company is supposed to compete against an American company when only our guy pays the tariff," Poilievre said.
BOOZE BAN
Canada's regional leaders said the United States has been particularly irritated by one retaliatory measure: the removal of US alcohol and wine from liquor stores.
Carney on Wednesday asked the provinces to restock US booze.
Some publicly agreed, but others voiced hesitance.
Quebec Premier Christine Frechette said she wanted to study the deal before agreeing to anything, while Manitoba's left-wing Premier Wab Kinew told reporters Trump appeared "weak" and suggested Canada should "fight".
Ontario Premier Doug Ford, one of Trump's most prominent critics during the trade war, has so far stayed quiet.
Ford controls the Liquor Control Board of Ontario, one of the largest individual purchasers of US alcohol products.
Carney has repeatedly told Canadians that relations with the United States have been forever changed, regardless of what happens with an individual trade deal.
He says the country needs to diversify and reduce its reliance on the United States, which currently accounts for roughly 70 per cent of Canadian exports.
Beyond the ongoing negotiations, the United States and Canada still have to agree on revisions to the North American free trade agreement, USMCA, which Trump declined to renew last month.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: One dead after Canada plane hits car
Article:
MONTREAL: One person has been killed in western Canada after a small passenger plane struck a vehicle while making an emergency landing on a road, police said.
The incident occurred on Thursday afternoon in Prince George, British Columbia, more than 700 kilometres (435 miles) north of Vancouver.
Images of the incident show the small aircraft on the side of a road, nestled on the grass next to a forested area.
"Police are saddened to confirm that there has been one fatality in this incident, an occupant of one of the vehicles," the Royal Canadian Mounted Police said in a statement.
It was not immediately clear if anyone on the plane was injured.

Title: TikTok to pay US$400m settlement in US children's privacy case
Article:
SAN FRANCISCO: TikTok and parent company ByteDance have agreed to pay US$400 million to settle a lawsuit with the US Department of Justice over claims that the video-sharing platform violated federal children's privacy laws, the department announced on Friday.
"Under the settlement, TikTok will pay US$300 million immediately and an additional US$100 million upon entry of an order vacating a prior consent decree entered against TikTok's predecessor, Musical.ly," the department said in a statement.
It is "one of the largest recoveries ever obtained" from a case involving the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA), the statement continued.
COPPA bars websites from gathering the personal information of children younger than 13 without parental permission.
The Justice Department and Federal Trade Commission jointly sued TikTok in 2024, alleging that it had placed the safety of millions of children in jeopardy by collecting their personal data without parental permission.
They claimed that TikTok allowed children to use the app while also collecting and using personal data from young users without informing their parents.
Even accounts created in a "Kids Mode" intended for users younger than 13 gathered email addresses and other personal information, the suit claimed.
In 2019, the US filed a COPPA lawsuit against an app called Musical.ly, which ByteDance bought in 2017 and then merged into TikTok.
TikTok did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
According to an ABC News report in May, the Trump administration was considering using the funds for ongoing "beautification" projects, which have included resurfacing the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, renovating the White House ballroom and building an arch.
It was not immediately clear what the settlement funds would be used for.
GLOBAL CRACKDOWN
The US settlement comes amid a growing global crackdown on the video app.
Brussels began a probe into TikTok in 2024 under the Digital Services Act (DSA) – a content law and major weapon in the EU's strengthened legal arsenal that it has deployed to rein in Big Tech in recent years.
In July, the European Union accused TikTok of failing to protect children through account settings that can expose them to risks such as cyberbullying and predatory behaviour, putting the company at risk of a large fine.
The EU said minors' accounts should only be visible to those they have given permission to. Children aged 13 and over can use TikTok.
"A high level of protection should not be an opt-in; it should be the default," EU tech chief Henna Virkkunen said in a statement at the time.
Under the DSA, children's account settings have, by default, the strongest safety and security protections.
"TikTok's account settings fail to meet this standard, as they expose minors' accounts and content too widely," the EU said in its preliminary view.
Britain's communications regulator also launched an investigation into TikTok in July.
The UK probe will look into whether TikTok is doing enough under UK law to protect children from harmful content.
"This investigation will seek to establish whether there are reasonable grounds to believe that TikTok has failed, or is failing, to comply with its legal obligations," Ofcom said in a statement.
It added that it would in particular look at TikTok's age-verification model.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Pentagon fires Stars and Stripes leaders after they criticise interference
Article:
WASHINGTON: The Pentagon on Friday fired the editor-in-chief and publisher of the Stars and Stripes newspaper, which has covered the US military since the Civil War, according to the publication's leadership, which spoke to US media.
The publication's editor-in-chief, Erik Slavin, told CBS News he was being fired for "insubordination" following an interview with the network in which he spoke about disagreements with the Department of Defence.
The department stated earlier this year that it was seeking to steer Stars and Stripes coverage away from "woke distractions".
Max Lederer, who has served as the publication's publisher since 2007 and had announced his retirement just three days earlier, was also notified that he was being terminated, according to CBS.
Stars and Stripes reporter Lara Korte said she too was sacked, posting on X: "Today, I was informed that the Department of Defence is firing me for insubordination after I told a CBS reporter that I work for Stars and Stripes – not the Pentagon, not any administration, and not any policy maker."
The separation notices came just days after the newspaper, which is partially funded by the Department of Defense but has long maintained editorial independence, reported on grim conditions for crew members aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln.
The story provoked fresh criticism of President Donald Trump's war against Iran.
The aircraft carrier had been deployed since before the Middle East war began in February. Last weekend, the military announced that a new carrier strike group had arrived in the region, and Trump said the Lincoln would be swapped out.
Slavin made waves last month when he pushed back against editorial interference by the Pentagon.
Asked on "CBS Sunday Morning" if he had any red lines he would not cross, Slavin responded: "'Don't run a perfectly accurate story, run this instead. Here it is, written by the Pentagon.' That would be a red line."
Lederer, the publisher, announced his retirement from the paper on Tuesday, to take effect September 30.
He chose to step down because he realised his philosophy of leadership and "understanding of the value and mission of Stars and Stripes" differed in "fundamental ways" from the Pentagon's plans for the organisation.
US Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth has been severely critical of the media since taking the helm in 2025, and the independence of Stars and Stripes and other military media has come under threat.
Shortly before Lederer announced his resignation, active-duty US Navy Captain William Urban was installed as military deputy to the publisher, a move interpreted by many, including Democratic lawmakers, as eroding the publication's independence.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Netherlands fines Uber US$960 million over driver account suspensions
Article:
AMSTERDAM: The Netherlands has fined ride-hailing giant Uber 825 million euros (US$960 million) for having deactivated drivers' accounts without informing them.
A spokesperson at the Dutch data protection authority on Friday confirmed the judgement, which had been agreed Monday.
The ruling is based on European data regulations which state that people should not "be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing."
The case relates to incidents that took place in Europe between 2020 and 2022.
It began with a complaint against Uber filed in France, but the case was heard in the Netherlands because the US car-booking giant's European headquarters are in Amsterdam.
Uber said it contests the decision and the "disproportionate" fine, and will appeal. --AFP
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Brazil's Lula urges tariffs resolution in call with Trump
Article:
BRASÍLIA: Brazilian President Luiz Inacio da Silva urged US President Donald Trump in a phone call Friday to resolve their countries' trade dispute, saying US tariffs were imposed on "baseless" grounds.
Washington imposed two new rounds of tariffs on the Latin American giant in July over alleged unfair trade practices, a move that has become a key campaign issue ahead of an October presidential election in Brazil.
Lula – who is seeking a fourth and final term in office – told Trump that the tariffs "negatively affect both Brazil and the United States" and that "to remain at the negotiating table is the best option for both countries," according to a statement from his office.
Relations between Trump and the leftist Lula have blown hot and cold in recent months, but diplomatic tensions have flared as the election approaches.
Trump has backed several victorious right-wing candidates in Latin America recently and is an ally of Brazil's jailed far-right former president Jair Bolsonaro, whose son Flavio is Lula's main rival in the election.
The statement from the Brazilian presidency said the conversation between Trump and Lula lasted an hour and 20 minutes and "took place in a friendly and cordial tone."
Lula, 80, has made national sovereignty a key theme of his campaign.
He said recently that if he spoke to Trump he would tell him: "Don't meddle in Brazil's affairs, especially regarding the election. If you do meddle, you'll lose."--AFP
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Sword-wielding attacker wounds at least two teens at Swedish school
Article:
STOCKHOLM: At least two teenagers were seriously wounded after a sword-wielding attacker entered a high school in central Sweden, authorities said, while media reported the perpetrator had been shot by police.
Regional healthcare director Jonas Cederberg told AFP two "seriously wounded" people had been admitted to hospital. A third person whose injuries had yet to be ascertained was in the process of being brought to hospital.
The two seriously wounded were boys between the ages of 12 and 17, one of whom was in emergency surgery though both were in stable condition, the healthcare authority said on its website.
"An assailant armed with a sword has entered Brinellskolan and wounded several people," the Fagersta municipality said in a statement, adding that the assailant had been detained by police.
Police said they had received reports of the attack just after 2pm (1200 GMT).
Students, just back from their summer holidays, were still in lockdown at the school more than three hours later, said public broadcaster SVT's reporter from the scene.
The local authority said a little later that the lockdown had been lifted.
The local authority did not specify how many people had been wounded but said in a statement that police were still searching the school and that several other schools in the area had been locked down.
The local authority postponed a news conference initially scheduled for 5pm, saying "a rescue operation" was still ongoing.
The motive for the attack was not immediately clear.
Aftonbladet newspaper reported that the attacker had been shot in the leg by police. It also cited unidentified sources as saying the attacker was an 18-year-old former student of the school.
Images on public broadcaster SVT showed multiple ambulances and police cars parked outside the school as well as a police helicopter.
The school has around 450 students, in a town of around 12,000 inhabitants.
In May, the municipality announced that students at Brinellskolan had been sent home following a threat to the school.
- 'SERIOUS INCIDENT' -
Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson told AFP in a written statement that "a serious incident has taken place today at a school in Fagersta, just after the summer holidays."
"There are reports of people being injured. We do not yet know what lies behind the attack, but we do know that the police are working extremely intensively," Kristersson said.
Magdalena Andersson, leader of the opposition Social Democrats, lamented the "terrible news" from Fagersta, in a post on X.
"My thoughts are with those affected and everyone involved," she said.
"When violence takes place at a school, I know it impacts everyone in our country. All of Sweden stands with Fagersta in this difficult time."
Sweden has suffered some high-profile attacks at educational institutions.
In February 2025, a 35-year-old man killed 10 people at an adult education centre in Orebro – Sweden's worst mass shooting.
Police said it had been motivated by the killer's wish to end his life because of financial and psychological woes.
In March 2022, an 18-year-old student stabbed two teachers to death at a secondary school in the southern city of Malmo.
And in October 2015, three people were killed in a racially motivated attack at a school in the western town of Trollhattan by a sword-wielding assailant who was killed by police.--AFP
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: UK, Canada, Australia slam Israel ending probe into aid worker killings
Article:
LONDON: Britain, Canada, and Australia on Friday condemned as "shameful" Israel's decision to close an investigation into the death of seven aid workers killed in Gaza in 2024.
The World Central Kitchen employees – three Britons, a dual US-Canadian national, a Pole, an Australian, and a Palestinian – died in a drone strike on their vehicle convoy after overseeing the unloading of a food aid shipment.
Israel's military called the incident a "tragic mistake."
"In the more than two years since, we have been pressing for Israel to swiftly and thoroughly consider the case and hold those responsible to account," the three nations said in a joint statement.
"The announcement by the IDF (Israel Defence Forces) on Aug 19 2026 that it would not pursue criminal investigations into this strike, without further explanation, is shameful," it said.
The incident in April 2024 sparked global outrage and renewed calls to ensure the safety of aid workers in Gaza.
"Announcing this decision on World Humanitarian Day, while the world honoured the courage and sacrifice of humanitarians, was particularly egregious," the joint statement added.
The Israeli military acknowledged a series of errors at various levels of command, but a preliminary investigation concluded on Wednesday that there was no "reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct."
"Israel extends its condolences to the families of the seven World Central Kitchen aid workers... who tragically lost their lives under deeply regrettable circumstances," Israel's foreign ministry posted on X on Friday.
It said the decision not to launch a criminal probe "was made by Israel's independent military prosecution authorities on the basis of strict professional and legal considerations."
"We remain committed to the safety of humanitarian personnel, compliance with international humanitarian law and preventing such tragedies from recurring," it added.
The US-based World Central Kitchen condemned the decision not to launch a criminal investigation, calling it "inconsistent with the full truth and deeply offensive."
It demanded an independent commission to investigate the airstrikes "because the IDF cannot credibly investigate its own conduct."
On Thursday, Australia expressed outrage at the closure of the investigation and summoned Israel's ambassador to the country.--AFP
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: US-sanctioned ICC head warns against 'demise of international rule of law'
Article:
TOKYO: International Criminal Court President Tomoko Akane of Japan warned on Friday against "the demise of international rule of law" after the United States targeted her with sanctions.
Washington sanctioned Akane and trial lawyer Abdoulaye Seye of Senegal on Tuesday as part of the Trump administration's campaign against what it calls a "corrupt and fatally politicised" body.
"The sanction against me this time was something I had anticipated to an extent, so I'm not surprised," Akane said in a statement released on X by her publisher Bungei Shunju.
"The important thing is not to let this be the beginning of the demise of international rule of law."
The measures bar Akane and Seye from entering the United States and from carrying out transactions in the US financial system.
Akane's statement – her first public comments since the sanctions – comes after the ICC on Wednesday called the US measures a "flagrant attack" on the court's independence.
The United Nations rights chief Volker Turk and top EU officials threw their support behind Akane and her institution.
Washington's latest move follows sanctions it imposed on several ICC officials, seen as largely in response to the court's investigations involving Israel, a US ally.
Japan has also objected to the sanctions on Akane, with the foreign ministry saying it "consistently supported the ICC... in its efforts to prosecute and punish the most serious crimes of concern to the international community and to uphold the rule of law."
Japan is the biggest funder of the ICC and a close US ally.
Established in 2002, the ICC prosecutes individuals accused of the gravest atrocities and acts as a last resort when countries do not have adequate legal systems to ensure accountability.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio earlier said in a statement, without providing examples, that the sanctioned "individuals have directly engaged in efforts by the ICC to investigate, arrest, detain, or prosecute officials whose government has not consented to ICC jurisdiction."
The United States signed the Rome Statute establishing the ICC but never ratified the treaty. Israel, Russia and China are not ICC members either.
In 2023, the ICC issued an arrest warrant for Russian President Vladimir Putin over the war in Ukraine, prompting Moscow to issue its own arrest warrants for senior court officials.
These included Akane, 70, an ICC judge since 2018 who was elected as the court's president in March 2024.
"Even if one judge were to die, we are easily replaceable, so there is really no value in targeting us," she said after the Russian announcement.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Indonesia arrests 10 Myanmar nationals following liquid meth bust
Article:
JAKARTA: Indonesia has arrested 10 Myanmar nationals in a drug bust involving 2.6 metric tonnes of liquid methamphetamine found on a ship sailing with a Tanzanian flag, authorities said at a press conference on Friday.
The drugs were found in a water tank and eight 200-litre drums hidden on top of a container on the ship, Indonesia's National Narcotics Agency chief Suyudi Ario Seto said.
Indonesia has strict drug laws, with some offences punishable by death.
"This is concrete evidence that narcotics crimes have evolved from solid forms into liquid forms to infiltrate the public lifestyle through the use of vapes or electronic cigarettes," Seto said.
He called for a total ban on vapes.
The joint operation, which also involved police and customs, originated in intelligence information analysed by the drug agency starting from December last year, with suspicions triggered by the vessel frequently changing its identity.
They finally intercepted it on Monday, Aug 17, as it was passing through the waters of the Riau Islands in western Indonesia.
Authorities said the group arrested on Monday has links with previous arrests earlier this month involving a ship carrying 1.3 tonnes of ketamine, also in Riau waters.
Most of the crew members on that vessel were also of Myanmar nationality.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Swiss man jailed for insulting Hindu holiday in Indonesia
Article:
DENPASAR: Swiss authorities said Friday they were providing consular support to a national sentenced to one year in prison in Indonesia for insulting a Hindu religious day while he was on holiday in Bali.
Luzian Andrin Zgraggen, 26, was sentenced on Thursday after being found guilty of crimes under an Indonesian law against online hate speech, I Wayan Suarta, a spokesman for the court in Denpasar, told AFP.
Zgraggen was arrested in March after he was reported to police over an Instagram post in which he used expletives while denigrating "Nyepi", the Hindu Day of Silence that marks the Balinese New Year.
On that day each year, the Hindu-majority island largely comes to a standstill, with work, travel, public entertainment and even electricity use discouraged for locals and tourists alike.
Zgraggen's crime was punishable by up to five years' imprisonment under the law.
But the court took into account his young age and good behaviour in court as mitigating factors.
In response to a query from AFP, the Swiss foreign ministry in Bern said it was aware of the case but could not provide further information for privacy reasons.
"The Swiss Embassy in Jakarta is in contact with the competent authorities and is providing support to the person concerned within the framework of consular protection," it said in a statement.
The ministry said consular services provided to Swiss citizens imprisoned abroad included informing them of "the possibility of a transfer to Switzerland" and verifying that they were kept in dignified conditions.
"In its general information for travellers, the FDFA (Federal Department of Foreign Affairs) emphasises in particular the need to respect local laws as well as religious and cultural customs," the statement added.
"The travel advice for Indonesia also mentions this point."
Bali attracts millions of foreign visitors each year but has seen several recent high-profile cases of misbehaving tourists.
In March, authorities on the island arrested two French nationals and an Italian for allegedly producing and distributing pornography, which is forbidden in the Muslim-majority country.
Last month, authorities barred two Dutch citizens from ever returning to the country for their role in allegedly organising a running event exclusively for foreigners.
Indonesia officially recognises six religions as well as indigenous beliefs.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Malaysia, Pakistan want Hormuz Strait kept open, safe amid Iran-US tensions
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia and Pakistan agree that the Strait of Hormuz must remain open and safe to ensure the smooth flow of international trade.
The position was conveyed during a phone call between Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim and his Pakistani counterpart Shehbaz Sharif today.
The two leaders discussed developments in Iran-US relations and stressed the importance of continued engagement to ease tensions.
"We exchanged views on current developments in the region and agreed that all tensions must be addressed carefully through dialogue and diplomacy to preserve regional peace and stability," Anwar said in a Facebook post tonight.
On bilateral ties, Anwar and Shehbaz agreed to intensify trade and economic cooperation, which still had significant potential, including expanding Pakistani meat exports to Malaysia.
"All commitments reached must be translated swiftly into tangible outcomes that benefit both countries. Malaysia will continue to support Pakistan as a friendly nation and an important partner," Anwar said.
Earlier, Shehbaz asked Anwar about his health.
Anwar said he appreciated Shehbaz's prayers as well as the flowers and fruit sent to him.
"I informed (Shehbaz) that I am currently recovering," he said.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Russian social network sues Apple over App Store removals
Article:
MOSCOW: Russian social network VK said on Friday that it had filed a lawsuit against Apple with the Moscow Arbitration Court, demanding that the company's apps be reinstated in the App Store, reported Sputnik/RIA Novosti.
According to court documents, VK LLC filed the claim with the Moscow Arbitration Court against United States (US)-based Apple Inc., Russian Apple Rus LLC and Ireland-based Apple Distribution International Ltd., although the subject and grounds of the claims have not yet been disclosed in the documents.
"In the lawsuit, VK is demanding that Apple return the company's apps to the App Store, restore users' ability to receive notifications from the apps and pay a penalty if the court's ruling is not enforced," the company said.
Apple unilaterally removed VK's apps from the App Store without warning, VK claimed.  – BERNAMA-Sputnik/RIA Novosti
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Malaysia, Pakistan sign treaty allowing prisoners to serve sentences at home
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia and Pakistan today signed the International Transfer of Prisoners (ITOP) Treaty, strengthening legal and security cooperation between the two countries.
Home Minister Datuk Seri Saifuddin Nasution Ismail said the treaty was signed with Pakistan's Interior and Narcotics Control Minister Syed Mohsin Raza Naqvi following his courtesy call on Pakistan Prime Minister Muhammad Shehbaz Sharif.
The signing ceremony was held at the Prime Minister's Office in Pakistan and witnessed by Shehbaz.
"This signing marks another important milestone in Malaysia-Pakistan bilateral relations, particularly in strengthening security and legal cooperation between the two countries," he said in a Facebook post today.
Saifuddin said the treaty was the outcome of five rounds of negotiations held since September 2025 involving the Home Ministry, Foreign Ministry, Attorney-General's Chambers, Malaysian Prisons Department and Royal Malaysia Police.
He said the Cabinet had also approved the treaty on May 13.
Under the ITOP, Malaysian prisoners held in Pakistan may be repatriated to serve the remainder of their sentences in Malaysia, while Pakistani prisoners serving sentences in Malaysia may be transferred to their home country to complete their sentences.
"This also enables them to undergo rehabilitation programmes in a more conducive environment that is suited to the mould and culture of their respective countries," he said.
Saifuddin said the signing added another legal instrument to the long-standing Malaysia-Pakistan relationship and reflected both countries' commitment to expanding cooperation that benefited their people.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: NST Leader: Plugging the gaps in border security
Article:
FOR decades,   drug cartels  have  developed sophisticated methods to evade detection, favouring  deep-sea transit and commercial container fraud because the bigger payloads mean bountiful profits.
Porous  borders and strategic positioning within the Strait of Malacca make  Malaysia and Indonesia lucrative markets and critical transit hubs for Golden Triangle syndicates.
Smugglers constantly diversify transport methods through trial and error — the "errors" being the busts made by  anti-narcotics police over the years. One enduring method relies on  drug mules.
Although they carry smaller payloads, there is no shortage of naive  individuals enticed by such a payday, willing to risk life and limb to deceive border authorities.
These drug mules fall into three categories. The first:   hazardous ingestion —  stuffing drugs into body cavities,   or  concealing liquid forms in flexible containers —  seems  outdated.
The second: strapping contraband to the  body or hiding  them inside medical aids like casts or orthopaedic braces.
The third: concealing drugs in everyday items to evade detection is what likely snared the  off-duty Malaysia Airlines second officer  on July 28 at Soekarno-Hatta International Airport, who was caught trafficking  25kg of ecstasy and methamphetamine worth  RM45 million in his luggage.
Nevertheless, the odds of detection are higher since law enforcement agencies use body scanners, digital radiography and refined profiling.
Prompted by  the pilot's brazen action, the cabinet approved 17 recommendations to tighten security, screening and risk management at Kuala Lumpur International Airport  and other   entry points.
The measures call for  targeted screening of high-risk flights, passengers, crew and baggage, alongside e-vetting and stricter access controls for flight crews, ground staff, vendors and  contractors in  restricted  areas. Drug testing  for aviation personnel, including pilots and cabin crew,  will also be further bolstered through pre-employment, periodic and random checks.
These drastic measures are commendable, but must avoid  creating  unnecessary inconvenience  for travellers entering and leaving the country.
They require clear  timelines and measurable outcomes; scanners, surveillance systems and risk-management tools are effective only if officers are properly trained and systems are regularly maintained and effectively deployed.
The primary goal must be structural border security, not just a knee-jerk reaction.
Tighter security is a given, but it seems that only a debacle is able to wake law enforcement up on the need for constant  vigilance. We must ask: was existing screening sufficiently robust before the co-pilot was caught?
While the new measures integrate multiple agencies tasked with securing Malaysia's borders, collective responsibility must now become second nature. If one agency fails, everyone fails.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Netanyahu calls Turkiye's Erdogan 'antisemitic dictator'
Article:
JERUSALEM: The office of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Friday called Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan an "antisemitic dictator" and vowed Israel would "continue to act forcefully against Turkiye's attempts to destabilise the region."
It comes days after Syria accused Israel of bombing an air base in the country's north, a short drive from the Turkish border, with Netanyahu later tacitly acknowledging the strike.
Netanyahu had said Turkiye was looking to establish a military presence there, but Turkiye has denied any visit to the site.
It also follows an announcement by Turkiye on Friday that it had sought an international arrest warrant for Netanyahu, accusing him of "genocide" linked to Israel's interception of an aid flotilla for Gaza.
"Israel has long been unimpressed by Turkiye's hypocrisy. Erdogan is an antisemitic dictator who massacred Kurds, supports the massacre of the Hamas, and oppresses his own people," Netanyahu's office said in a statement.
It added that Israel would "continue to act forcefully against Turkiye's attempts to destabilise the region and against any threat to its security."
On Tuesday, Syria accused Israel of striking a disused military air base near the northwestern city of Aleppo that was damaged during the civil war and has been out of service since 2012.
Israel said a Turkish military delegation had recently visited the site, with a Syrian war monitor saying it was part of efforts to reactivate the base.
On Thursday, Turkiye denied having any military presence at the base and vowed to continue "resolutely" supporting Syrian sovereignty.
In an English-language statement on Friday, Netanyahu's office accused Erdogan of seeking "to extend his aggression against Israel into Syria."
"Israel will not tolerate it," the statement said.--AFP
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Harry's UK return raises more questions than answers
Article:
DOZENS  of questions swirled on Thursday as Prince Harry prepares to move back to the United Kingdom with his wife and children, six years after his departure sparked a bitter rift with the royal family.
In a surprise move, Harry and Meghan "plan to leave the United States by the end of the month to settle in a private, non-royal residence, which is said to be located outside London",
The Daily Telegraph
reported on Wednesday.
Media outlets, including the BBC, reported the couple's two children, Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5, had already been enrolled in a British school for the start of the school year early next month.
But many questions remain.
Some commentators pointed out that Harry and Meghan's US adventure has largely failed to live up to expectations.
"Meghan's cookery series didn't go well. They haven't managed to cooperate successfully... with Netflix. And also, they lost Spotify," royal commentator Richard Fitzwilliams said.
"I think they've not been a success in Hollywood and I think this is one way to change things, and change things before William becomes king."
The couple may also be concerned over reports that Prince William "might remove their (royal) titles", he added.
Another commentator, Ed Owens, said King Charles III's younger son was keen to reconcile with his father and family.
Harry and Meghan met the king last month during a brief visit to the UK, the first time in four years the couple's children had met their grandfather.
"There's a sense that visit went well... so now might seem an opportune moment," Owens said.
After stepping back as working royals in 2020, Harry, 41, and Meghan, 45, known as the Duke and Duchess of Sussex, eventually settled in Montecito, California.
It has been reported that the couple have chosen a new house in the UK, but it will not be one of the many royal residences.
Fitzwilliams said the rural Cotswolds area of western England, where Harry spent time as a child at his father's private Highgrove House residence, appeared to be a possibility.
They also spent some time last month with Harry's uncle, Charles Spencer, in the ancestral home of Althorp, where his mother Princess Diana grew up and is buried.
The late Queen Elizabeth II made it clear to Harry and Meghan before her death in 2022 that there was no "half-in/half-out" option under which they could pursue commercial ventures while being working royals. There appears to be no change to that position from Buckingham Palace.
"Their podcasts, lifestyle shows and entrepreneurial activities are seen as incompatible with the ethos of royal work, which is considered to be done for the greater good, not for financial gain," said sociologist Nathalie Weidhase of the University of Surrey.
Harry is patron of a number of UK charities and remains involved with the Invictus Games for wounded veterans, which he founded and which will be held in Birmingham next year.
The couple's reported initial US$100 million deal with Netflix was last year replaced with a reduced agreement to develop film and television projects for the streaming giant.
Meghan also launched a lifestyle and consumer-products brand, As Ever, last year.
The couple are not popular with the public, with a YouGov poll revealing only 22 per cent of Britons had a positive opinion of Meghan and 33 per cent for Harry.
Relations with Harry's family nosedived in March 2021 with a no-holds-barred interview with American talk show hostess Oprah Winfrey.
The rift deepened further with the publication in January 2023 of Harry's tell-all memoir
Spare
.
While bridges have been rebuilt with Charles, Prince William, the heir to the throne, and Harry remain estranged.
The Daily Mail
tabloid reported that William would be "apoplectic".
"There is a very deep rift. He feels Harry has betrayed him," Fitzwilliams said.
Harry has said he did not feel safe bringing his family to Britain after losing a court battle over government-funded police protection.
Jennie Bond, a former BBC royal correspondent, told Sky News it was "extraordinary that he feels suddenly that he can bring his wife and children to the UK when a year ago he couldn't see any way of doing that because of the issues over security".
The writer is from AFP
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: The haze is man-made, the suffering is shared
Article:
Two heavy afternoon downpours earlier this week in Kuching did little more than give the city short respites from the chocking haze enveloping it and much of Sarawak.
The Air Pollution Index for the city is again creeping up to hazardous levels.
There is much anger over the air quality, something beyond the control of anyone in the state.
A politician in Serian — the nearest main town to the Kalimantan border — even suggested that  reparations be requested from Indonesia, where the haze, as a result of uncontrolled forest fires, mostly originates.
The haze has been rather subdued in recent years. That it has now returned with a vengeance may have something to do with the extended El Nino dry weather effect this year.
The worst haze occurred some three decades ago, when everything looked like the grainy visuals one sees on television.
A federal minister then, clearly in equal measures of exasperation and desperation, went to the extent of implausibly suggesting the mass evacuation of everyone out of Sarawak!
Then Indonesian president Suharto issued a public apology later.
The then annual haze became a subject tackled by Asean — and rightly so, since it respects no international borders when it hits.
While Malaysians rightly bemoan the dismal air quality in swathes of the country, let us perhaps also spare a thought for Indonesians living in Kalimantan and Sumatra who must be bearing the brunt of the  haze now, largely through no fault of theirs either.
Are these Indonesians just as powerless as us in demanding firm action from their government to put a stop to this recurring nightmare once and for all?
Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto has lately been making quite a show of putting the country's biggest conglomerates on notice for what is perceived to be rather selfish and irresponsible behaviour.
Many of these conglomerates also own huge tracts of oil palm plantations in Kalimantan, where much of the forest fires have been deliberately started to economise on land-clearing costs.
We should cheer firm and stern action by Indonesian authorities against such corporate negligence, even if some of the plantations are owned and operated by Malaysian conglomerates.
Even as Malaysians express collective and rather impotent dismay over this man-made smoky air blowing our way from Indonesia, we need to also have some empathy for Indonesians who are having to tolerate the same, only worse.
Empathy must also extend to our neighbours who suffer greater natural disasters than we do.
Indonesians on the island of Flores have just faced a high-intensity earthquake, which, like others the country experiences with some regularity, bring death and destruction.
Manila in the Philippines is currently mostly inundated following excessive rainfall.
The poor living in the city's slums are, as usual, the ones who bear the brunt as their rickety homes get flooded or swept away.
But even as we sympathise and empathise with our neighbours over natural disasters, we must be resolute in  demanding firm action against those causing man-made forest fires and the resulting haze.
The writer views developments in the nation, region and the wider world from his vantage point in Kuching
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Health Ministry sets 3 priorities for 2027 Budget
Article:
PUTRAJAYA: The Health Ministry (MOH) has identified three main clusters for Budget 2027 — strengthening healthcare services for the people, enhancing national resilience, and promoting social justice and development for all.
The ministry said the priorities were discussed during its Budget 2027 Engagement Session here today.
"MOH also stressed that every allocation must be outcome- and impact-oriented, rather than merely focusing on the amount of expenditure.
"Each proposal must clearly identify the problem to be addressed, the beneficiary groups, the intended changes and the methods for measuring its effectiveness," it said in a social media post today.
According to the post, Health Minister Datuk Seri Dr Dzulkefly Ahmad, in his speech at the engagement session, stressed that Budget 2027 must be used as an instrument to strengthen the country's healthcare system.
He said the approach was important to ensure every allocation channelled to MOH delivered meaningful outcomes and impact for the people.

Title: Penang Health Dept apologises over long waits at hospital ER
Article:
GEORGE TOWN: The Penang Health Department has apologised for long waiting times at Penang Hospital's Emergency and Trauma Department following a viral video posted on social media.
The department said it took note of the video, which circulated on the night of Aug 20, highlighting lengthy waiting times at the hospital's emergency department.
Penang Health director Dr Zulhizzam Abdullah said patients at the department were managed through a triage system based on the severity of their medical conditions, rather than their arrival time.
He said patients were categorised into three zones — Red for critical cases requiring immediate treatment, Yellow for semi-critical cases requiring urgent medical attention and Green for non-emergency cases involving mild or non-critical symptoms.
"During peak periods, including late at night, treatment priority is given to Red and Yellow cases.
"This may result in longer waiting times for Green Zone patients when there is a simultaneous surge in critical cases," he said in a statement tonight.
Dr Zulhizzam said overall waiting times could also be affected by the time required for blood tests, further examinations and assessments by relevant specialist teams.
As a short-term measure to ease congestion, Penang Hospital is upgrading space at its Outpatient Department block to allow for the expansion of treatment areas and integration of patient flow at the emergency department.
The upgrading works are expected to be completed by the end of this year and will provide a more comfortable waiting environment, particularly for elderly and special-needs patients.
For the longer term, construction of the hospital's Women and Children's Block is underway and is expected to be completed by the end of 2027.
The new block will include a larger and more comfortable Emergency and Trauma Department, while another block under the Specialist Clinics and Wards project is expected to be completed in 2029.
Dr Zulhizzam said the new infrastructure would provide greater treatment capacity, modern facilities and a more conducive working environment to accommodate patient demand in Penang.
He said the state Health Department and Penang Hospital remained committed to providing equitable and quality healthcare.
Those experiencing mild or non-emergency symptoms were also encouraged to seek treatment at the nearest health clinic to help reduce congestion at emergency departments.
